content:
In #38329 I'm tightening down the public API of AlgebraicClosure.
Does someone know why we care so much about the Field instance, and in particular the ratCast components and its friends?

Can we just put a field instance on this and move on? Or will that make someone downstream very sad?

cc @Yaël Dillies @Eric Wieser

Why public def AlgebraicClosure?

I would be interested to see the final state of this PR. I would love to understand what the module system is supposed to be doing in a practical example. Clearly the definition of algebraic closure as a quotient of a huge multivariable polynomial ring by an ideal defined using the axiom of choice should be hidden from downstream files.
If I remember correctly this was very slow at some point (maybe during the port), and we changed definition various times. If it now works I think we can just go with the field instance.

Kevin, what you are thinking of is @[expose]. Public means that you can refer to a def/thm outside of the module it is defined in, expose means that you can unfold a definition. There is a section in the language reference that explains it very nicely
I think it's reasonable to completely hide the actual definition of AlgebraicClosure.

What about the following: the only public interface is a theorem: for any (F : Type u) [Field F] there is (Fbar : Type u) [Field Fbar] [Algebra F Fbar] [IsAlgClosure F Fbar] plus some more necessary universal property. Since this is a theorem, it does not carry any data. The actual AlgebraicClosure and field instance is Exists.choose, Exists.choose_spec, etc. etc.
In this way the actual definition of AlgebraicClosure is completely hidden.

This reminds me that while writing PR #28013, I replaced the original let and haves with

  obtain ⟨K, _, _, _, _, _⟩ : ∃ (K : Type) (_ : Field K) (_ : Algebra ℚ K) (_ : Algebra K ℂ)
      (_ : IsScalarTower ℚ K ℂ), IsSplittingField ℚ K (P.map (algebraMap ℤ ℚ)) :=
    ⟨IntermediateField.adjoin ℚ ((P.map (algebraMap ℤ ℚ)).rootSet ℂ),
      inferInstance, inferInstance, inferInstance, inferInstance,
      IntermediateField.adjoin_rootSet_isSplittingField (IsAlgClosed.splits _)⟩

which made type checking much faster.
I've now gotten rid of all @[expose]. But there is weird downstream breakage that I need to fix as a consequence.
What goes wrong if we hide the definitions of AlgebraicClosure type and its field instance? What proofs are relying on the details of the construction?
Smells to me like such proofs should be lifted to work for any IsAlgClosed field
@Artie Khovanov There's not much that goes wrong, see the PR.
I made the same mistake as Kevin and confused public with expose
Doesn't hiding the implementation make it impossible for projects like FLT to add new instances like StarRing inherited from the quotient implementation?
(since import all isn't legal outside mathlib)

Maybe this is more a complaint that import all shouldn't be banned in this way, which seems hostile to ForMathlib directories

edit: this only applied before 4.28.0 and lean4#12045
I think this is straightforwardly a trade-off of encapsulation
In this case you can presumably get the instance from it being an algebra over a star ring, right?

Maybe, but if you added the result to mathlib you'd presumably want to inherit the instance. It's then frustrating that the version you want to write in mathlib is illegal in ForMathlib. edit: this only applied before 4.28.0

I can't think of any mathematically relevant facts that doesn't follow from "algebraically closed algebraic extension."
Maybe cardinality?

Eric Wieser said:

Maybe, but if you added the result to mathlib you'd presumably want to inherit the instance. It's then frustrating that the version you want to write in mathlib is illegal in ForMathlib.

Yes, agreed. I guess I'm saying this is an unavoidable downside of encapsulation - in a sense it's what it means to encapsulate.
It would be avoidable by removing the ban! There are still huge benefits to forcing users to opt in with import all without restricting who can do that edit: this only applied before 4.28.0
That's totally fair

In #37854 I attempted the same kind of thing for SplittingField, hiding it's definition entirely. In doing so, I encountered some zsmul instance diamond that would need to be fixed. I presume this is a similar problem as with AlgebraicClosure. It was partially for this reason that I opened #38036.

I don't understand what I could possibly want from the definition. If I know (a) it's algebraic over K (b) it's algebraically closed then I know it up to isomorphism and I can prove everything else from this.

Well, to summarise the above

  1. You need the definition for a fact like cardinality (or I guess you can duplicate the work)
  2. Proofs might get more complicated downstream if we can't just derive instances from the construction
  3. Sometimes defeq matters

Cases 1. and 2. only need to exist in the definition file itself and in downstream for_mathlib files, which is why the restriction on import all sucks. Case 3. is more of an issue since it might come up in code that superficially only needs the external interface.
But otoh, case 3 is what we're trying to fight. It's by design. Defeq matters, but it also hurts. And we're trying to find ways to make it matter less.
Whenever you have an instance diamond the caller always needs to be able to unfold things enough to check they're defeq
Yep exactly - this is a big barrier to encapsulation as it stands
Is that not the case with what is happening in #38329 ?

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

In #37854 I attempted the same kind of thing for SplittingField, hiding it's definition entirely. In doing so, I encountered some zsmul instance diamond that would need to be fixed. I presume this is a similar problem as with AlgebraicClosure. It was partially for this reason that I opened #38036.

Btw, for splitting field there's the option of simply adjoining all of the roots in the algebraic closure. I took a stab at this a long time ago (#21000), but it didn't seem to improve things (performance-wise) back then, but maybe now it could be worth looking at again after AlgebraicClosure is tidied up?

I see a lot of people talking about import all restrictions but I don't think there are such restrictions anymore (since lean4#12045), e.g. I can simply

module
public import Mathlib
import all Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Floor.Defs

#print FloorRing.ofBounded.eq_def

even though docs#FloorRing.ofBounded is marked @[no_expose] (even when I'm not in the mathlib code base).
Yes, sorry for the outdated information here

Eric Wieser said:

Whenever you have an instance diamond the caller always needs to be able to unfold things enough to check they're defeq

However you do not need the whole Field instance to be exposed for this to happen. What @Johan Commelin should do is to make intermediate unexposed AddCommGroup instances etc... and use them to build the Field instance.

It would be easier if there was a way to unexpose subterms, something like an unexpose() elaborator. That way, we could unexpose specific fields, rather than relying on the fact that the fields we want to unexpose come from earlier typeclasses

Well, I'm not sure that I should be doing that. I think that doesn't scale.
If this diamond issue is a real problem, then I think this should either be fixed in core, or we should come up with some metaprogramming to create the intermediate instances for us.

But first I need to understand why such diamonds would arise in the first place.

Yaël Dillies said:

is to make intermediate unexposed AddCommGroup instances etc

This doesn't help with multiple inheritance, instead you make each function implementing one of the operators unexposed

I don't understand the discussion here yet. How can we possibly end up with two Field structures on AlgebraicClosure K which need to be unfolded to check they're defeq? Isn't the proposal to make something analogous to

constant AlgebraicClosure (K : Type*) [Field K]
constant i : Field (AlgebraicClosure K)
attribute [instance] i

etc? But just without the constants?
The problem is checking e.g. that the zsmul coming from the field structure is defeq to the smul coming from the SMul R k → SMul R (AlgebraicClosure k) in the special case R := ℤ.

I doubt that what you write is an instance (I don't think it makes mathematical sense) but if we have the analogous Algebra instance (which does make sense) then I now see the problem. Does the Algebra instance exist? Should it? More and more in FLT we're not relying on instances like this (which can lead typeclass inference down incorrect paths), we are instead just assuming [Algebra R (AlgebraicClosure K)] [IsScalarTower R K (AlgebraicClosure K)] (well, we're doing it for AdeleRing K but same principle)
@loogle Algebra _ (AlgebraicClosure _)
:shrug: nothing found

Kevin Buzzard said:

I doubt that what you write is an instance (I don't think it makes mathematical sense)

docs#AlgebraicClosure.instSMulOfIsScalarTower is the real one
No idea why loogle didn't find docs#AlgebraicClosure.instAlgebra
Yeah the latter is the one. I have no idea what the former is all about!

And my objection to it is that if typeclass inference wants to find Algebra (AlgebraicClosure K) (AlgebraicClosure K) then if you're not careful it tries to find Algebra (AlgebraicClosure K) K (which doesn't exist) and the next thing you know it's trying to find NormedAddCommGroup K and everything has gone haywire and you've lost hundreds of thousands of heartbeats. It's for this sort of reason we had to increase the priority of Algebra.id
The former gives you the action of Units Rat on AlgebraicClosure Rat etc
To me it sounds like the problem is not that it tries to find Algebra (AlgebraicClosure K) K, but that this is somehow very slow to fail

I'm not sure how this is any different to trying to find Algebra R[X] R[X] and then getting stuck looking for Algebra R[X] R. These things should just fail quickly, and if they don't then something is wrong elsewhere
Well this is why I occasionally start banging on about decoupling algebra from all the other hierarchies, this would accelerate the failure
I agree that it's the same issue. I'm just wondering aloud whether these are good instances but perhaps you're right and the problem is elsewhere
I think if you declare Algebra A B -> Algebra A (F B) a bad instance for some functor F, then you pretty much throw away everything that is great about typeclass search

I think #38329 in its current form is:

  1. An improvement over the status quo.
  2. Not perfect. Eg it introduces 3 #adaptation_notes.
  3. The best I can make it given my skills and availability.

I've been looking at how to do this better, though I haven't figured it out yet. But I would be against merging it in its current form, because the inferInstanceAs are creating exposed definitions where the value does not have the right type in the exported environment. So it seems reasonably likely to me that when this bug in inferInstanceAs gets fixed, these instance declarations will get broken.

Artie Khovanov said:

I can't think of any mathematically relevant facts that doesn't follow from "algebraically closed algebraic extension."
Maybe cardinality?

You don't need the any actual construction to understand the cardinality of an algebraically closed algebraic extension LLL of a field KKK. Every element of LLL is a root of a nonzero polynomial in K[T]K[T]K[T], and any such polynomial has finitely many roots in KKK, so that Card(K)≤Card(L)≤sup⁡(Card(K),ℵ0)\mathrm{Card}(K)\leq \mathrm{Card}(L)\leq \sup(\mathrm{Card}(K),\aleph_0)Card(K)≤Card(L)≤sup(Card(K),ℵ0​). Using that finite fields are not algebraically closed, you get the right inequality is an equality.
Sure. But that's repeating a lot of the argument of the construction.
It's also a very short argument and very readable -- far more readable, in fact, than something which explicitly uses our construction of alg closure.

Artie Khovanov said:

Sure. But that's repeating a lot of the argument of the construction.

Really? The above argument works for any algebraic extension; it doesn't require algebraically closed.
Both fair points!
